title.$t: The Flood That Drowned the World: Wrangel Island’s Last Mammoths and the Birth of Sumer

content.$t:
The flood that drowned the world after the Ice Age, the first civilization, and eight mammoths who kept their kind alive for six thousand years on a small Arctic island.

This article was first published in Nepali on Shilapatra on September 7, 2026 (Bhadra 22, 2083 BS). This is the author’s own English translation.

The article’s header as published on Shilapatra.
Two refugees of one flood: what the rising seas did in Beringia and the Persian Gulf (created with Claude).

As the seas rose at the end of the Ice Age, the world’s last mammoths, trapped on their way to Alaska, kept their kind alive on one small island for the next six thousand years. The same water had turned the people who once made their homes where the Persian Gulf is today into refugees.

In one corner of the world, a small herd of mammoths was stranded on an island. In another, the first human refugees from the water dug canals and gave birth to the world’s first civilization.

In short

  • As the Ice Age ended, the ice melted and the world’s seas rose by about 120 meters.
  • Beringia, the grassland bridge between Siberia and Alaska, drowned about 11,000 years ago. People, mammoths, camels and horses had all crossed it.
  • About eight mammoths were trapped on Wrangel Island. Their descendants outlived the mainland mammoths by some six thousand years, until around 1750 BCE.
  • The same water drowned the Ur-Shatt Valley, where the Persian Gulf is now, pushing its people north into southern Mesopotamia.
  • There, refugees from the south met Ubaid farmers from the north. Canals, administration and the first city, Eridu, followed.

The world of twenty thousand years ago was not like today's world.

When the ice began to melt twenty thousand years ago, the whole world changed.

The melting came to everyone alike.

When the Ice Melted, Twenty Thousand Years Ago

At the peak of the Ice Age, much of the northern hemisphere lay buried under ice. Canada, Scandinavia and northern Europe were covered by sheets of ice up to two kilometers thick.

But the ice was not everywhere. Cold alone is not enough for ice to build up; it also needs snow. Siberia was cold, but extremely dry. So even at the height of the Ice Age, no ice sheet ever formed there.

Instead, a vast open plain stretched to the south and east, from Spain through Siberia all the way to Alaska. We know it as Beringia.

It was not an empty place. For thousands of years, this open plain was the playground of a giant: the woolly mammoth. If you have seen the film Ice Age, its hero, Manfred, or Manny, is a woolly mammoth.

Beringia, the mammoths’ playground (image from the internet).

This ice began to melt twenty thousand years ago. The meltwater had to go somewhere. And it went into the sea. After the end of the Ice Age, sea levels around the world rose by a hundred and twenty meters, and the rise went on until about 6,000 years ago.

The sea did not rise everywhere at once. The first place it touched was that same grassland joining Siberia and Alaska.

The Busiest Road on Earth, Joining Asia and America

For most of the Ice Age, Siberia and Alaska were joined. Today that land lies under the sea, but in the Ice Age it was dry ground. Mammoths used this route to move back and forth.

This route joining Asia and America was not the narrow strip we imagine. The “bridge” was a vast grassland. In places more than a thousand kilometers wide, it was grazed by herds of mammoth, bison and wild horses.

An artist’s impression of a woolly mammoth (digital image from the internet).

And Ice Age people followed those herds onto the open plain, about 60,000 years ago. We often imagine bands of hunters trailing mammoth herds from Asia into America. But the story of how people reached America is not that simple.

For their first thousands of years there, the Ice Age hunters stayed in Siberia and Beringia. Ice blocked the way into Canada, and they could go nowhere until it opened. Only after the ice melted and the way opened did they reach America, about sixteen thousand years ago. Within a few thousand years, they had reached the southern tip of the Americas.

Beringia had connected Asia and America for hundreds of thousands of years, long before mammoths or Homo sapiens existed.

Camels and Horses: Born in America, Raised in Asia

Beringia wasn't just a one-way route for migration from Siberia to America. Many species that first evolved in America crossed the same route into Asia, Eurasia, and Africa, where they continued evolving as natives.

The desert camel is the best example. It may sound surprising, but the camel is an American animal. It evolved in North America and spent its first forty million years there.

Some of the camel’s ancestors crossed Beringia, heading west, and reached Asia. The Bactrian camels of Central Asia and the camels of the Arabian Desert are their descendants. Some went south and became llamas, alpacas, and their kin. Those that stayed behind in America all died out about twelve thousand years ago.

In other words, the Arabian camel, the animal that made civilization’s first long journeys possible, was itself an immigrant that came from America to Asia at the end of the Ice Age.

The horse’s story is much the same. The horse also evolved in America. Horses crossed Beringia into Asia, spread out across Central Asia, and died out in their own homeland. America’s native horses vanished about ten thousand years ago, at the end of the Ice Age. For horses to return, America had to wait eight thousand years for Columbus and the other Spanish ships.

For hundreds of thousands of years, the Beringian bridge was the busiest road on Earth. Mammoths and people heading east, camels and horses heading west. Then the ice melted and came as water. Slowly at first, very slowly, and then, from about 14,000 years ago, all at once.

Beringia was low-lying, and the sea drowns low ground first. First the coast went under. Then the plain narrowed. Then it broke into pieces. About 11,000 years ago the bridge disappeared completely, and Siberia and Alaska were separated for good.

A bridge that had joined Asia and America for hundreds of thousands of years sank beneath the sea within a few thousand.

When the Grass Ran Out on the Siberian Steppe

In the last ten thousand years of the Ice Age, not only the sea rose.

First, the world itself warmed. The world of ten thousand years ago was about five degrees Celsius warmer than the world of twenty thousand years ago. For the mammoths enjoying their cold Siberian playground, it proved to be a death sentence.

As temperatures rose, the air grew more humid, the frozen ground thawed, and water with nowhere to drain turned into a bog. Where grass had grown for thousands of years, scrub and moss now sprang up, along with new bushes and birch trees never seen there before.

An adult mammoth needs about two hundred kilograms of grass a day, and that much grass could no longer be found anywhere. As the grasslands shrank, the herds broke up into small groups. We hunters added to the pressure. The thawing permafrost may also have spread new diseases.

Whatever the causes, the result was the same. The last mammoths in Siberia drew their final breaths about ten thousand years ago.

But eight mammoths stranded on a small island in Beringia kept their kind alive for another six thousand years, far from the rest of the world.

The Mammoths’ Last Home: Wrangel Island

At the northern edge of Beringia there is a patch of high ground. As the water rose, the plain around it drowned, and that ridge became an island above the water.

About 10,000 years ago, some eight mammoths were cut off from the Siberian mainland on this island. They had walked there before the ridge became an island, and then, finding no way back, they stayed.

Today we know it as Wrangel Island. The water trapped them, and the very island that trapped them kept them alive.

The water trapped eight woolly mammoths, and the very island that trapped them kept them alive for another six thousand years.

Mammoths that had vanished everywhere else in the world survived only on this island. The herd grew from eight animals to as many as eight hundred at one point. For thousands of years, their numbers averaged around four hundred.

They had not chosen the island. The sea had stopped them there. There was no way out. The land was what it was. They could eat only as much grass as grew. There was no way to get more.

The same grass, the same rocks, generation after generation; for six thousand years they waited.

Wrangel Island (image from the internet).

While the mammoths lived on their island, people in another corner of the world were being driven out by the same water. The people who reached the southern plains of Mesopotamia around 6,500 BCE—and who would later build the world’s first civilization—were refugees chased away by the rising sea, by this first flood.

The Fertile Valley That Drowned at the Other End of the World

Where the Persian Gulf lies today, a green, fertile valley once stood. The sea where the Tigris and Euphrates now meet did not exist during the Ice Age. The two rivers met and continued south as a single river for about another thousand kilometers, passing through the narrow mouth of Hormuz before emptying into the Gulf of Oman. This Ice Age river is called the Ur-Shatt.

The fertile valley that drowned to form the Persian Gulf (image from the internet).

When the sea stood a hundred and twenty meters lower than it does today, this valley was home to ancient people. It was very different from the surrounding land and far more fertile. To the east lay the dry mountains of Iran; to the west, the Arabian Desert; and between them lay this green plain, built from the soil the river brought down.

Of the people who left Africa and spread across the world via the Red Sea, one group made this valley its home about sixty thousand years ago. There were lakes on both sides of the river. There were marshes. Reeds grew. There were date palms. The river had fish, the marshes had birds, and animals came to the banks to drink.

Life was not hard. No one had to go far for food. You could catch fish, trap birds, eat marsh roots and tender reed shoots. The dates grew by themselves. The animals came to drink on their own.

For thousands of years, people stayed right there. The same river, the same marsh, the same dates. Generation after generation.

But the same water that drowned Beringia was now about to arrive here too.

An Apocalypse Within a Single Generation

At first, the sea rose slowly, about a centimeter a year. Around 14,000 years ago, the rate tripled.

Little by little, the water swallowed the Ur-Shatt Valley. The valley was extremely flat, and on flat land water does not rise upward; it spreads sideways.

In this valley built by the river, the sea began to move inland a meter every three days—about a hundred and twenty meters a year. Do the arithmetic, and that’s a kilometer every ten years. A thousand kilometers in eight thousand years.

In other words, for the first time, a person could watch the flood eat away at the land within a single lifetime.

The rock a child had stood on to fish would be underwater by the time he was grown. Paths turned into marsh. The date palms that survived withered in salt water. Every generation had to move a little higher and relocate its homes. A few generations later, their descendants had to do it all over again.

The rock a child had stood on to fish would be underwater by the time he was grown.

And the valley kept narrowing. People who had spread across it for thousands of years were now crowded onto shrinking land. One day, even that narrow strip disappeared. The water completely drowned the Ur-Shatt Valley.

By around 6,000 BCE, the Persian Gulf had already formed, and one high piece of land left above it survives today as Bahrain.

The First Story of a Flood That Drowned the World

The story of the people of Sumer begins with this very flood. Their myths say that the world of their ancestors was one day drowned by waters that brought a great deluge.

They called present-day Bahrain Dilmun, their ancestral land. A clean, pure land where no one fell sick and no one grew old. It was there that Enki first made humankind.

One day, the gods of this garden paradise grew angry and decided to wipe out the people around them. But Enki, the god of fresh water, disagreed. He taught the people there how to escape.

“Tear down your house, build a boat,” Enki told Ziusudra.

Then the water came. Seven days and seven nights. Everything was gone. Only Ziusudra’s boat survived.

This story of a great flood drowning the world was later recorded in Babylon as the flood of Utnapishtim. Then it appeared as Noah’s flood in the Hebrew Bible, and later in the Christian Bible and the Muslim Quran, spreading across the world.

The same story echoes in our own Samudra Manthan and in the Matsya avatar. It may be the oldest story humans have kept telling. But the deluge their ancestors lived through was something else altogether.

A seven-day flood on the rivers of Mesopotamia is nothing new. But the water their ancestors faced did not come for just seven days. It came over thousands of years, and it never stopped. Fathers moved on from where their grandfathers had left off, and sons from where their fathers had left off. For hundreds of generations, every generation saw the same thing: The water rises, the land shrinks, and we must move north.

The water rises, the land shrinks, we must move north.

The rising sea drowned marshes, lakes, and forests. It swallowed whole villages. People were crowded into ever-narrower spaces, and before the sea could take its next step, they moved from one place to the next, learning to live in each new place.

This migration north in search of higher ground continued from 6,000 to 5,500 BCE. Carrying the story of their world lost beneath the water, the people of Sumer first reached the coasts of southern Iraq.

The World’s First Civilization, Born in the Least Likely Place on Earth

But southern Iraq was no paradise when they arrived. It was perhaps the least suitable place in the world for the first civilization to begin. There was no stone, no forests to cut for timber, no mines, and no metal anywhere—only a blazing sun, hot winds blowing wildly, and sandy marshes into which your feet sank.

But there were two rivers, and here they worked like an elixir of life. Flowing down from the north with soil from Turkey’s Taurus Mountains, these rivers kept Mesopotamia's riverbanks fertile for hundreds of thousands of years.

Around those very mountains in Turkey, whose soil the Tigris and Euphrates carried downstream, people first developed farming more than ten thousand years ago.

The Ubaidas, Who Followed the Rivers from Turkey to Mesopotamia

Former hunters who had only just learned to farm began spreading everywhere in search of farmland. Around 6,500 BCE, some bold people from the early farming Samarra culture and the northern foothills followed the rivers south. Archaeologists call this time the Ubaid period.

As they moved downriver, they made the river their companion. Where there were no trees, they cut the tall marsh reeds and bound them into huts. In the shade of the date palms by the river, they began planting pomegranates and figs. Later, they made the potter’s wheel and learned to work clay with it.

But those early people of the Ubaid still lived at nature’s mercy. They were limited to wherever the river reached. They had not yet learned to build fields or boats.

Sumer and Ubaid: Two Worlds Meet

These people coming down from the north met the refugees coming up from the south. Two groups, from two different worlds. And water had brought both there.

We call them the Ubaid civilization because archaeologists found their pottery at a place called Ubaid. But who they were and where they came from are still unclear. Take this as an example: Homo sapiens reached Egypt some twenty thousand years after reaching Nepal.

The Ubaid people who came down from the north were people of the soil. They knew when to sow, when to harvest, and how to store grain after harvest. They had sickles; they had pots.

Those who came from the south were people of the water. The marsh was nothing new to them. Where fish get caught in a net, when to cut the reeds, which roots are good to eat, and which month the birds arrive—no one had to teach them these things. Most important of all, they remembered how water rises, where it goes, and where it stops. We call them the Sumerians.

Had these two kinds of knowledge stayed apart in southern Iraq, perhaps neither would have amounted to much.

The group from the north brought farming; the group from the south knew how to build canals, and together they carried farming across the desert of southern Mesopotamia.

These two communities, brought together after the Ice Age, started the world’s first civilization. Begun in the barren desert of southern Iraq by the people of Sumer and Ubaid (later known as the Akkadians), this civilization went on to rule that part of Mesopotamia in one form or another for the next four thousand years and taught humankind the ABCs of civilization.

That beginning of civilization came from turning streams into canals and stretching farmland into the desert.

Administration, Born from Turning Rivers into Canals

Farming grew, and villages grew bigger. Officials were needed to look after the canals linking the rivers. Someone had to assign the officials; someone had to give the orders. The workers digging the canals had to be paid.

So, the need to dig canals and manage water gave birth to the world’s first administration.

Through canals, villages and administration, the world’s first city was born here too. At Eridu, in today’s southern Iraq, some 10,000 people lived in 5,400 BCE. This may well be the world’s first city.

Ruins of the main temple at Eridu (photo from the internet).

Born in the marshes between two rivers, Sumerian civilization endured in Mesopotamia for about four thousand years. Over those four thousand years, it changed humankind forever. The Sumerians laid the foundations for the bread we eat, the beer we drink, the arithmetic we use, and the cities we live in.

The End of Sumer

But the cycle of time and nature is merciless. The very soil and water that gave Sumer life eventually turned against it: once the water stopped coming, the salt left in the soil and desert sand poisoned their civilization.

Sometime around 1900 BCE, after the Elamites burned Ur, Sumerian civilization ended forever. After nearly four thousand years of glorious history, it vanished completely. The people who gave the world writing were themselves wiped entirely from human memory.

In that same place, around 1,700 BCE, the kingdoms of Babylon rose, and Hammurabi was born. By then, the kings of Sumer had already become legendary figures.

About three hundred years later, Sumerian civilization had vanished from memory itself. Only the name of Sargon the Great of Akkad would survive, and the kings of Sumer were already just gods of ancient times.

The Last Breath of the Ice Age Refugees

Far from southern Iraq, in another corner of the Earth, a different wait was going on.

Those last mammoths, imprisoned by the sea, were still alive. For six thousand years, on the same narrow island, among the same grass and rocks, they had lived on, generation after generation.

When the Sumerians built the world’s first city, those mammoths were there. And when Sumerian civilization collapsed completely and disappeared into the depths of history, they were still there, breathing.

About three hundred years after the first great civilization disappeared into the dust, around 1750 BCE, the world’s last mammoth breathed its last in the cold wind of Wrangel Island.

One group of refugees left after ushering in a new age of human history; the other took an entire Ice Age with it.

This was the story of the greatest flood the human world has ever seen. We have had to see with our own eyes the unimaginable damage melting ice can cause. The world’s temperature is rising every day, and in the Himalayas, it is rising twice as fast. What will happen if the ice remaining on Earth’s third pole melts? I hope that, starting now, we can prepare to prevent the loss of lives and, as far as we can, property too.

Frequently asked questions

Why did mammoths survive so long on Wrangel Island?

Rising seas cut Wrangel off from Siberia about 10,000 years ago. No hunters reached it, and a small herd lived on the island’s grass for some six thousand years. The last mammoths died about 4,000 years ago.

What was Beringia?

The land exposed between Siberia and Alaska when Ice Age seas were much lower. This grassland, in places more than a thousand kilometers wide, drowned about 11,000 years ago and became the Bering Strait.

Did a flood really fill the Persian Gulf?

Yes. In the Ice Age, most of the Gulf was dry land, crossed by the combined Tigris and Euphrates. Between about 14,000 and 6,000 years ago, the sea slowly filled it. That this inspired the flood myths is a hypothesis, not a proven fact.

Where did the Sumerians come from?

It is still debated. One hypothesis says people displaced from the drowning Gulf moved north and became the Sumerians. Other scholars think Sumer grew out of the local Ubaid-period population.

What was the world’s first city?

Many consider Eridu the first city. Settled around 5400 BCE, it was also where, according to the Sumerians themselves, kingship first came down to earth.

title.$t: Kushim and Sukkalgir: The First Names Ever Written

content.$t:
Before poetry, epics, and laws came accounting. And the numbers were already in our hands. Sumerian civilization, rising from Mesopotamia’s clay and riverside reeds, gave the world its first writing system and its oldest surviving literature.

The Oldest Name in History Belonged to a Man Counting Barley

This article was first published in Nepali on Shilapatra on August 22, 2026 (Bhadau 6, 2083 BS). This is the author’s own English translation.

Accounts before poetry: how writing began, at a glance (created with Claude).

Have you ever wondered what the oldest human names we have found are? We tend to imagine a queen or king, a god or goddess, or an extraordinary hero. But the oldest named woman and man known to history come from this very city, and they were two ordinary people.

Five and a half thousand years ago, Kushim counted barley in a storehouse in Uruk; a few generations later, Sukkalgir was written down as someone’s property.

This is their story.

In short

  • Writing began as accounting, not poetry: the oldest tablets from Uruk (c. 3400–3100 BCE) record barley, goats and beer.
  • The name Kushim appears on eighteen of those tablets. It may be the oldest name we can read, though it could be a job title rather than a person.
  • Sukkalgir, listed around 3100 BCE as one of two slaves owned by Gal-Sal, is the first woman whose name we can read.
  • The popular story of “Nisa”, Kushim’s female supervisor, has no scholarly basis.
  • Our sixty-second minute and 360-degree circle come from Sumerian counting in sixties, which you can do on your finger joints.

The oldest names in history belong to no king or god. Kushim counted barley in a storehouse in Uruk five and a half thousand years ago; Sukkalgir is the first woman whose name was ever written down, recorded as someone’s property. From counting to sixty on our fingers to clay tablets and Gilgamesh, this is the story of how writing began.

The Story of Gilgamesh, the World’s Oldest Epic

‘He who saw the deep, who knew the foundations of the earth, who was wise in all things.’

This is how the oldest literature of human civilization begins. The Epic of Gilgamesh, written in Uruk around 2100 BCE, tells the story of Gilgamesh, king of Uruk. Written nearly a thousand years before the oldest parts of the Bible, Gilgamesh tells stories of kingship, grief, immortality, and a flood that drowned the whole world.

The story of Gilgamesh is not a story of victory. It is the story of a king who set out to conquer death and, in the end, came home to his own city, exhausted.

The Epic of Gilgamesh, the flood story (1200 BCE, Assyrian tablet, British Museum).

According to the story, Gilgamesh was two parts god and one part man, carrying both a god's restlessness and a man's weakness. He knew that he would die. And so, he does what people afraid of death do.

Gilgamesh cuts through the cedar forest the gods had forbidden anyone to enter. He fights a monster. He crosses the waters of death. While he sleeps on a riverbank, a snake steals the immortality he was about to win. Gilgamesh returns to Uruk empty-handed. And finally, standing before the walls of his own city, he says:

‘Behold the walls of Uruk, climb up and walk on them. Examine the foundation, inspect the brickwork. Is it not made of kiln-fired brick? Did not the gods themselves lay out its plan?’

– The Epic of Gilgamesh (1200 BCE, Assyrian tablet)

This is how the world’s oldest story ends. Not with the gods pleased, not with a throne regained. A tired king, the walls he built himself, and a quiet understanding: the city I built will outlive me by far.

Gilgamesh stood before the walls of Uruk sometime around 2700 BCE. The walls and stones where he stood crumbled into ruins over time. The city was erased from memory, but what it gave human civilization is far greater than Gilgamesh’s walls of stone and mud.

Five hundred years before Gilgamesh, Uruk already stood in southern Mesopotamia as the world’s first great city. Two hundred years before that, someone in Uruk began patting wet clay flat in their palm, pressing a piece of reed into it, and making marks. Marks that would last far longer than stone and walls.

A stroke. A number. A word.

Numbers Before Words

Before Gilgamesh, before the cedar forest and the walls of Uruk, long before every story we have heard about the ancient world, numbers came first. And no one had to invent numbers. They were already in our bodies, hiding in the fingers of our hands.

Raise your right hand and spread it open. With your thumb, touch and count the joints of the other four fingers. Each finger has three joints. Four fingers, three joints. Without lifting the other hand, one hand gets you to twelve.

Once you reach twelve, fold down one finger of your left hand. Each time you reach twelve, fold one finger. When all five fingers are folded, how far have you counted?

Five times twelve. Sixty.

This is how it began. Not in a palace or a temple, but in the hands of ordinary people who had to keep everyday accounts. No one announced this system of counting in sixties. It was already in all our bodies: anyone, anywhere, even someone who knew nothing else, could count on their fingers.

The counting system begun by Mesopotamian civilization (created with Claude).

This is how the city of Uruk was built in Mesopotamia; this is where Sumerian civilization began. Those numbers are still with us. The Sumerians didn’t just begin writing; they buried the counting they began so deep in the bones of civilization that we still haven’t let go of it.

We still use that mark for five when tallying: four strokes struck through the middle. Sixty seconds in a minute. Sixty minutes in an hour. Three hundred and sixty degrees in a circle. The clock hanging on the wall still tells time the way the people of Sumer counted on their fingers five thousand years ago.

The clock on the wall still tells time the way the people of Sumer counted on their fingers five thousand years ago.

But sixty is not writing. Sixty is counting. And for a very long time, hundreds, perhaps thousands of years, counting was enough. Writing came much later. And it began not with words but with pictures.

Clay, Reeds and the First Marks

The first stars of human civilization began to shine in Uruk around 3400 BCE. Another Sumerian poem written a little after the Gilgamesh stories, Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta, credits the invention of writing to the king of Uruk (3400 BCE), Kullaba, who had more messages than a messenger could carry.

‘The messenger’s mouth was heavy, and he could not repeat the message. Then Kullaba patted some clay into a tablet and set words upon it. Before Kullaba did so, there had been no custom of setting words on clay.’

– Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta (c. 2000 BCE)

The people of Sumer had plenty of two things: the river mud beneath their feet and the reeds growing on its banks. A scribe would pat a lump of clay into a tablet, much like today’s mobile phone, cut a reed into a point, and press that point into the clay to make marks. The wedge shape gave the world’s oldest script its name: cuneiform, meaning wedge-shaped.

From pictures to wedges: samples of the earliest signs (created with Claude).

The first marks were pictographs, simple pictures anyone could understand by looking. A picture of a fish meant fish. A drawn circle meant cattle. A jar meant oil. This system, which first appeared around 3400 BCE, is called proto-cuneiform.

The first records are dry: lists of goats, measures of barley, rations of beer. But their meaning was enormous. For the first time, writing freed information from depending on memory alone, moving it onto clay tablets that could travel anywhere. The first letters were not written for the gods. Nor for kings. They were written for grain.

In the Mesopotamian heat, clay dried hard and stayed that way. That is why those first marks survived, piled in old storerooms, buried under centuries of ruins. When archaeologists dug up tablets written in Uruk at that time, five thousand years later, they could still read the records.

Eighteen Surviving Tablets, and One Name

In that memory, eighteen tablets have survived. Just eighteen tablets recovered from the ruins of Uruk, inscribed sometime between about 3400 and 3100 BCE.

They were not laws. They were not hymns. Nor were they royal proclamations carved to last forever. They are receipts. Ledgers. The daily account books of a busy storehouse preserved for five thousand years. And on all eighteen tablets, the same two signs are inscribed: ‘Ku.’ ‘Shim.’

Kushim. The oldest name we find in history.

Kushim was not a king, a warrior, a priest, or even a mason who built walls. Kushim was an ordinary man who kept the temple’s accounts: a storekeeper standing at the storehouse door, counting what came in and what went out. His name repeats on all eighteen tablets in the same neat hand.

The first letters were not written for the gods. Nor for kings. They were written for grain. In his famous book Sapiens, Yuval Noah Harari reads one of the oldest messages our ancestors left behind like this:

‘29,086 measures barley, 37 months, Kushim.’

Probable meaning: ‘A total of 29,086 measures of barley were received over the course of 37 months. Signed, Kushim.’

Harari adds: ‘The earliest texts of history contain no philosophical insights, no poetry, legends, laws, or even royal triumphs. They are humdrum economic documents, recording the payment of taxes, the accumulation of debts and the ownership of property.’

Kushim’s tablet, Uruk, 3400–3000 BCE. Photo: Schøyen Collection MS 1717.

Even so, saying this much goes beyond what we can prove. There is almost no context around those signs, and it is still not settled whether Ku-Shim refers to a person, a title, or a whole institution. Kushim may have been a man. Kushim may have been a post.

One of those eighteen tablets may preserve history’s very first accounting error. The barley total is wrong, off by fifteen measures, and the mistake is found hastily corrected on the back of the tablet.

That mistake, buried for five thousand years, does what no monument can. It makes Kushim a person like us. Someone we recognize. Not a legend, just an ordinary man who got his sums slightly wrong in the rush of work.

Kushim wasn’t writing history. He was counting barley, doing his job.

Kushim wasn’t writing history. He was counting barley, doing his job.

The First Woman Written into History

Another tablet from a generation or two after Kushim’s dates to about 3100 BCE. It records a master and two slaves he bought.

Two slaves of Gal-Sal: En-pap X and Sukkalgir.

Three people in four words: a master, and the two people he enslaved. Part of En-pap’s name is broken off, and we still can’t read it. Only half his name survives. Linked with his is another name, Sukkalgir, which is beyond doubt.

In the archaeological record so far, she is the first woman whose name we can read. Not a goddess. Not a queen. Not a priestess carved on a temple wall.

Property.

Two slaves of Gal-Sal. Oriental Institute Museum, Chicago, OIM A2513 (photo: Jean Grant).

This is what the record gives us, and it is worth pausing on. The first time a woman’s name was written down anywhere in the world, it was written to keep account of whose property she was.

The first time a woman’s name was written down anywhere in the world, it was written to keep account of whose property she was.

She didn’t write it. She had no say in it. What she was like, how she came to belong to someone else, how long she lived, we don’t know. We know her name, and we know that Gal-Sal had enslaved her.

And Then, About Nisa

In many places that tell the story of the first people in history, you will find Nisa named as the first woman: Kushim’s supervisor, the woman who signed his ledgers, the first woman whose name was written down in history.

It’s a good story. But there is no scholarship beneath it. Wherever she appears, readers usually guess the sign might be ‘Nissa,’ not Nisa. No one has evidence she was a woman at all. Somewhere between one telling and the next, she seems to have been invented.

The truth is harder. It usually is.

From Pictures to Letters

Civilization in Sumer was only just beginning. By 3000 BCE, Uruk had already become the largest city of the ancient world, home to some 50,000 to 100,000 permanent residents.

Within a few generations of Kushim, those pictures had begun to change. Slowly the pictographs grew simpler. Need slowly turned the pictures etched into clay tablets into letters.

In the Mesopotamian heat, a scribe copying hundreds of documents a day has no time to draw a fish every time he needs to say fish. The picture gets simpler. The sign rotates. An ox’s head turns into a few strokes that no one would recognize as an ox.

By 3000 BCE, the script had moved entirely away from pictures to wedge-shaped impressions pressed into clay at an angle, what we now call cuneiform. The number of signs fell from more than fifteen hundred to about six hundred.

When Letters Began to Carry Sounds

Then someone realized: what if the signs pressed into clay stood for sounds? The picture of a fish standing not for a fish, but for the sound of the word ‘fish.’ The picture of a head standing not for a head, but for the syllable that word makes.

And if a sign could stand for a sound, it could be used for any word with that sound. And if signs could represent any word, then written tablets could carry any idea at all.

But this novelty brought something else with it: narrowing access. Only a class of trained scribes could read and write these new signs. A profession was born. A quiet hierarchy settled around the written word, and the world was never the same again.

Because, for the first time, knowledge outlived speech and memory. The clay dried, and the letters survived. That is why we can still read their epics and hear the echo of their music. People could learn from kings and writers who had died hundreds of years before they were born. Authority could be handed down not only by speaking but in writing. Knowledge no longer had to be kept in memory alone; it could be built upon.

Sumer’s technology was only just beginning. This was the starting point of the human civilization that spread across Mesopotamia.

In the End, the Same Walls Again

A few centuries after Kushim got his barley sums wrong, scribes in the same city pressed the story of a king into clay. A king who went to the edge of the world and came back empty-handed. Who stood before his own walls and understood his own impermanence.

Kushim’s barley was eaten long ago. Uruk’s walls are now only ruins. Gilgamesh has been dead for five thousand years. But their names remain. The Epic of Gilgamesh was written six hundred years after Gilgamesh died, and a thousand years later, the same story gave birth to the Torah, the Bible, and the Quran.

And among the earliest names we have found is a woman’s name too: Sukkalgir.

The first time a woman’s name was written anywhere in the world, she was recorded as someone’s property. She didn’t write it. She had no say in it. A claim in a bill of sale: property, nothing more.

Five thousand years later, we can still read Kushim, En-pap and Sukkalgir. A man who counted barley. A man of whose name only half survives. And a woman whose name was written down by someone counting his property.

That is what writing did: it preserved memory. It preserved not only the powerful, but also the careful. And it preserved the powerless too.

Frequently asked questions

What is the oldest name in recorded history?

Probably Kushim. The name appears on eighteen accounting tablets from Uruk dated between about 3400 and 3100 BCE. Scholars are still not sure whether it names a person or an office.

Who is the first named woman in history?

Sukkalgir. A tablet from around 3100 BCE records her as one of two slaves owned by a man called Gal-Sal.

Why are there 60 minutes in an hour?

The Sumerians counted in sixties. Counting the 12 finger joints of one hand, including the thumb, and marking each dozen on the five fingers of the other brings you to sixty. The system passed through Babylon to our clocks and circles.

When was cuneiform invented?

Picture-writing (proto-cuneiform) began in Uruk around 3400 BCE. By about 3000 BCE, those pictures had become wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay at an angle: cuneiform.

Was Nisa the first named woman in history?

No. The “Nisa” story is widely repeated online, but it lacks scholarly basis, and no evidence shows the name even belonged to a woman.

title.$t: कुसिम र सुक्कलगिर: इतिहासमा लेखिएका पहिला नाम

content.$t:
कविता, महाकाव्य र कानुनभन्दा पहिले हिसाब आयो । अनि, अंकहरू मान्छेकै हातमा थिए । मेसोपोटामियाको माटो र नदी-किनारको निगालोमाथि उभिएको सुमेरको सभ्यताले संसारलाई पहिलो लेखन प्रणाली दियो, सबैभन्दा पुरानो बाँचेको साहित्य दियो ।

यो लेख पहिलो पटक २०८३ भदौ ६ गते शिलापत्रमा प्रकाशित भएको थियो।

कविताभन्दा पहिले हिसाब: लेखाइको सुरुवात एक नजरमा (Created with Claude)।

कसैले सोच्नुभएको छ, हामीले अहिलेसम्म भेटेका सबैभन्दा पुराना मानव नामहरू के थिए ? हामी कोही रानी-राजा, देवी-देवता वा कोही असाधारण महामानव भनेर सोच्न पुग्छौँ । इतिहासमा अहिलेसम्म नाम भनेर थाहा पाएको महिला पुरुष यही शहरबाट आउँछन्- दुई साधारण मान्छे ।

आजभन्दा साढे पाँच हजार वर्षअघि उरुकको एउटा गोदाममा जौ गन्ने- कुसिम, र उसको केही पुस्तापछि कसैको सम्पत्ति भनेर नाम लेखिएकी- सुक्कलगिर ।

यो उनीहरूको कथा हो ।

छोटकरीमा

  • लेखाइ कविताबाट होइन, हिसाबबाट सुरु भयो। उरुकका सबैभन्दा पुराना पाटी (स.पू. ३४००–३१००) मा जौ, बाख्रा र बियरको हिसाब छ।
  • कुसिम नाम अठारवटा पाटीमा भेटिन्छ। सायद यो हामीले पढ्न सक्ने सबैभन्दा पुरानो नाम हो, तर मान्छेको नाम हो कि पदको, टुङ्गो लागेको छैन।
  • स.पू. ३१०० तिरको पाटीमा गल-सलका दुई दासमध्ये एक भनेर लेखिएकी सुक्कलगिर नाम पढ्न मिल्ने पहिली महिला हुन्।
  • कुसिमकी हाकिम ‘निशा’ को चर्चित कथाको कुनै अध्ययनको आधार छैन।
  • एक मिनेटमा ६० सेकेन्ड र वृत्तमा ३६० डिग्री सुमेरको साठीमा गन्ने तरिकाबाट आएका हुन्।

गिल्गामेसको कथा- संसारको सबैभन्दा पुरानो महाकाव्य

'जसले गहिराइ देख्यो, जसले धरतीको जग चिन्यो, जो सबै कुरामा बुद्धिमान् थियो ।'

मानव सभ्यताको सबैभन्दा पुरानो साहित्य यसरी सुरु हुन्छ । उरुकमा सनपूर्व (स.पू.) २१०० मा लेखिएको गिल्गामेसको महाकाव्यले उरुकका राजा गिल्गामेसको कथा भन्छ । सबैभन्दा पुरानो बाइबल लेखिनुभन्दा झण्डै एक हजार वर्षअघि लेखिएको गिल्गामेसमा राजा हुनुको, शोकको, अमरत्वको र संसारै डुबाएको बाढी सबैको कथा समेटिएको भेटिन्छ ।

गिल्गामेसको कथा कुनै जितको कथा होइन । मृत्युलाई जित्न हिँडेको एक राजा अन्त्यमा थाकेर आफ्नै शहर फर्केको कथा हो यो ।

गिल्गामेसको महाकाव्य, बाढीको कथा (ई.पू. १२००, एसिरियन ट्याब्लेट, ब्रिटिस म्युजियम) ।

कथाअनुसार, गिल्गामेस दुई भाग देवता र एक भाग मान्छे थियो । देवताको बेचैनी र मान्छेको कमजोरी, दुवै बोकेको । उसलाई थाहा थियो, आफू मर्छु भनेर । अनि, मृत्युदेखि डराउने मान्छेहरूले जे गर्छन्, उसले पनि त्यही नै गर्छ ।

गिल्गामेस, देवताले छिर्नै नहुने भनेको देवदारको (सेदार) जंगल चिर्छ । दानवसँग लड्छ । स्वर्ग-नर्कको पानी तर्छ । नदीको किनारमा सुतेका बेला उसले भेटाउन लागेको अमरत्व सर्पले खोसेर लगिदिन्छ । गिल्गामेस रित्तै उरुक फर्कन्छ । अनि, अन्त्यमा आफ्नै शहरका पर्खालअगाडि उभिएर भन्छ,

'हेर उरुकका पर्खाल, त्यसमाथि उक्लेर घुम । त्यसको जग जाँच, इँटा राम्ररी नियाल । के त्यो भट्टीमा पोलेको इँटाले बनेको होइन ? के त्यसको नक्सा भगवान्‌ले नै कोरेका होइनन् ?'

–गिल्गामेसको महाकाव्य (स.पू. १२००, एसिरियन ट्याब्लेट)

संसारको सबैभन्दा पुरानो कथा यसरी नै सकिन्छ । न देवता खुसी भएर, न सिंहासन फिर्ता पाएर । एउटा थाकेको राजा, आफैँले बनाएको पर्खाल, अनि एउटा चुपचाप बुझाइ- मैले बनाएको शहर मभन्दा धेरै बाँच्नेछ ।

गिल्गामेस उरुकका पर्खालअघि स.पू. २७०० को कुनै वर्ष उभिएको थियो । गिल्गामेसले उभिएको पर्खाल र ढुंगा समयसँगै खण्डहर बने । शहर सम्झनाबाटै मेटियो, तर यो शहरले मानव सभ्यतालाई दिएको देन गिल्गामेसको ढुंगा र माटोको पर्खालभन्दा धेरै ठूलो छ ।

गिल्गामेसको समयभन्दा पाँच सय वर्षअघि नै उरुक संसारको पहिलो महानगर भएर दक्षिण मेसोपोटामियामा उभिइसकेको थियो । उरुकमा त्यसको दुई सय वर्षअघि नै कसैले भिजेको माटो हातमा थपथपाएर त्यसमा निगालोको टुक्रा गाडेर चिनो बनाउन सुरु गरिसकेको थियो । ढुंगा र पर्खालभन्दा धेरै टिक्ने चिनो ।

                                                    एउटा धर्को । एउटा अंक । एउटा शब्द ।

शब्दभन्दा पहिले अंक

गिल्गामेसभन्दा पहिले, देवदारको जंगल र उरुकको पर्खालभन्दा पहिले, पुरानो संसारबारे हामीले सुनेका सबै कथाभन्दा धेरै अगाडि- सुरुमा अंकहरू आए । अनि, अंक कसैले बनाउनु परेन । हाम्रो शरीरमै थिए, हातका औँलाहरूमा लुकेर बसेका ।

आफ्नो दाहिने हात उठाएर फैलाउनुहोस् । बुढीऔँलाले बाँकी चार औँलाका गाँठा छामेर गन्दै जानुहोस् । हरेक औँलामा तीन-तीन गाँठा हुन्छन् । चार-औँला, तीन-गाँठा । अर्को हात नउठाईकनै एउटै हातमा बाह्र पुग्छ ।

एकपटक बाह्र पुगेपछि देब्रे हातका औँला एक-एक गर्दै खुम्च्याउँदै जानुहोस् । हरेकपटक बाह्र पुग्दा एक औँला, पाँच औँला खुम्चिँदा कति पुग्छ ?

पाँच गुणा बाह्र । साठी ।

सुरुवात यसरी नै भएको हो । दरबारमा होइन, मन्दिरमा होइन- दैनिक हिसाबकिताब राख्नुपर्ने साधारण मान्छेको हातबाट । साठी गन्ने यो प्रणाली कसैले घोषणा गरेर सुरु गरेको होइन । हामी सबैको शरीरमा पहिलेबाटै थियो- जहाँसुकै, जोसुकैले, केही नजाने पनि हातका औँला गन्न सक्थ्यो ।

मेसोपोटामियाको मानव सभ्यताले सुरु गरेको हिसाब प्रणाली (Created with Claude) ।

मेसोपोटामियामा, उरुक शहर यसरी नै बन्यो, सुमेरको सभ्यता यहीँबाट सुरु भएको थियो । ती अंकहरू हामीमाझ अझै छन् । सुमेरियनहरूले लेखाइ मात्रै सुरु गरेनन्, आफूले सुरु गरेको हिसाबलाई सभ्यताको हाडमै यसरी गाडिदिए, हामीले अझै छोड्न सकेका छैनौँ ।

गन्ती गर्दा चार धर्सो कोरेर बीचबाट काट्ने पाँचको त्यो चिनो हामीले अझै प्रयोग गरिरहेका छौँ । एक मिनेटमा साठी सेकेन्ड । एक घण्टामा साठी मिनेट । वृत्तमा तीन सय साठी डिग्री । भित्तामा झुण्डिएको घडीले अहिले पनि पाँच हजार वर्षअघि सुमेरका मान्छेले औँलामा गनेकै तरिकाले समय देखाइरहेको छ ।

भित्तामा झुण्डिएको घडीले अहिले पनि पाँच हजार वर्षअघि सुमेरका मान्छेले औँलामा गनेकै तरिकाले समय देखाइरहेको छ ।

तर, साठी लेखाइ होइन । साठी गन्ती हो । अनि धेरै लामो समय, सयौँ सायद हजारौँ वर्ष, गन्ती नै पर्याप्त भइरह्यो । लेखाइ धेरैपछि आयो । त्यो पनि शब्दबाट होइन, चित्रबाट सुरु भएको थियो ।

माटो, निगालो र पहिलो चिनोहरू

मानव सभ्यताका पहिला ताराहरू उरुकमा स.पू. करिब ३४०० तिर चम्कन सुरु भएको हो । गिल्गामेसको कथाको केही समयपछि लेखिएको अर्को सुमेरियन काव्य एन्मेर्कर र आरात्ताका राजाले लेखाइको आविष्कारक उरुकका राजा (स.पू. ३४००) कुल्लाबालाई दिन्छ- जोसँग हुलाकीले बोकेर पुर्‍याउन सक्नेभन्दा धेरै सन्देश थिए ।

“हुलाकीको मुख गह्रौँ भयो र उसले सन्देश दोहोर्‍याएर भन्न सकेन । त्यसपछि कुल्लाबाले छेउको माटो थपथपाएर पाटी बनाए, अनि त्यसमाथि शब्द राखिदिए । कुल्लाबाले त्यसो गर्नुअघि माटोमाथि शब्द राख्ने चलन थिएन ।”

- एन्मेर्कर र आरात्ताका राजा (~स.पू. २०००)

सुमेरका मान्छेसँग दुई कुरा प्रशस्त थिए- खुट्टामुनिको नदीले बनाएको हिलो माटो र किनारमा उम्रिने निगालो (रिड) । लेखक (स्क्राइब)ले माटोको डल्लो थपथपाएर अहिलेको मोबाइलजस्तै पाटी बनाउँथे, निगालो काटेर चुच्चो बनाउँथे, अनि त्यही चुच्चो माटोमा घुसारेर चिनो कोर्थे । त्यही चुच्चो आकारको नामबाट संसारको सबैभन्दा पुरानो लिपिको नाम बन्यो- क्युनिफर्म, अर्थात् किलाकार ।

सुरुका चिनोहरू पिक्टोग्राफ थिए, जोसुकैले हेरेर बुझ्ने सिधा चित्र । माछाको चित्रले माछा जनाउँथ्यो । कोरिएको गोलोले गाईवस्तु । घैँटोले तेल । पहिलोपटक स.पू. ३४०० तिर देखा परेको यो प्रणालीलाई प्रोटो-क्युनिफर्म भनिन्छ ।

चित्रबाट किलाकार- सुरुका अक्षरका नमुनाहरू (Created with Claude) ।

सुरुका अभिलेखहरू सुक्खा छन्- बाख्राको सूची, जौको नाप, बियरको बाँडफाँट । तर, त्यसको अर्थ विशाल रह्यो । लेखाइले पहिलोपटक सम्झनामा मात्र भर नपरी सुचनालाई माटोको पाटीमा सारेर सबैतिर पुग्न मिल्ने बनाइदियो ।

मेसोपोटामियाको तापमा माटो सुकेर कडा हुन्थ्यो र त्यसरी नै बाँचेर बस्थ्यो । त्यसैले ती पहिला चिनोहरू बाँचे- पुराना भण्डारमा थुप्रिएर, शताब्दीऔँको भग्नावशेषमुनि पुरिएर । उरुकमा त्यही बेला लेखिएका पाटीहरू पाँच हजार वर्षपछी पुरातत्त्वविद्हरूले खोतल्दा, ती अभिलेखहरू अझै पढ्न मिल्ने गरी बसेका थिए ।

बचेका अठार पाटी, अनि एउटा नाम

त्यही, सम्झनाभित्र अठार वटा पाटी बाँचेका छन् । उरुकको भग्नावशेषबाट निकालिएका जम्मा अठार पाटी- करिब स.पू. ३४०० देखि ३१०० बीचमा कोरिएका ।

ती कानुन थिएनन् । भजन थिएनन् । पछिसम्म रहिरहोस् भनेर कुँदिएका राजकीय घोषणा पनि होइनन् । ती भरपाइ हुन् । खाता हुन् । पाँच हजार वर्षसम्म जोगिएर बसेको एउटा व्यस्त गोदामको दैनिक हिसाब खाता । अनि, ती अठारैवटा पाटीमा उही दुई चिनो कोरिएका छन् । 'कु' । 'सिम' ।

कुसिम । हामीले, इतिहासमा भेटाउने सबैभन्दा पुरानो नाम ।

कुसिम राजा थिएन, योद्धा थिएन, पुजारी थिएन, पर्खाल बनाउने डकर्मी पनि थिएन । कुसिम मन्दिरको हिसाब खाता राख्ने साधारण मान्छे थियो- गोदामको ढोकामा उभिएर के भित्रियो, के बाहिरियो भनी गन्ने भण्डारे । उसको नाम अठारवटै पाटीमा उही सफा हस्ताक्षरमा दोहोरिन्छ ।

पहिला अक्षरहरू देवताका लागि लेखिएनन् । राजाका लागि पनि लेखिएनन् । ती अन्नका लागि लेखिएका हुन् । युवाल नोआ हरारीले आफ्नो चर्चित पुस्तक सेपियन्समा हाम्रा पुर्खाले छोडेका सबैभन्दा पुराना सन्देशमध्ये एकलाई यसरी पढेका छन्:

पहिला अक्षरहरू देवताका लागि लेखिएनन् । राजाका लागि पनि लेखिएनन् । ती अन्नका लागि लेखिएका हुन् ।

                                                '२९,०८६ नाप जौ, ३७ महिना, कुसिम ।'

सम्भावित अर्थ: 'सैँतीस महिनाको अवधिमा उनन्तीस हजार छयासी नाप जौ भित्रियो । हस्ताक्षर, कुसिम' ।

हरारी थपिदिन्छन्- 'इतिहासका पहिला लेखोटमा न कुनै दार्शनिक ज्ञान छ, न कविता, न कथा, न कानुन, न त राजाको विजयगाथा नै । ती त कर तिरेको, ऋण थुप्रिएको र सम्पत्ति कसको हो भन्ने टिपेका निरस कागजपत्र मात्रै हुन् ।

कुसिमको ट्याब्लेट उरुक, स.पू. ३४००-३००० । फोटो: स्कोयन संग्रह MS 1717 ।

यद्यपि, यति भन्नु हामीले प्रमाणित गर्न सक्नेभन्दा बढी हो । ती चिनोका वरिपरि सन्दर्भ लगभग भेटिँदैन र कुसिम भन्नाले एउटा मान्छे, कुनै पद, वा पूरै संस्था जनाएको हो भन्ने अझै टुङ्गो लाग्न सकेको छैन । कुसिम मान्छे पनि हुन सक्छ । कुसिम पदको नाम पनि हुन सक्छ ।

ती अठार पाटीमध्ये एउटामा सायद इतिहासकै पहिलो हिसाबको गल्ती जोगिएको छ । जौको जोड बिग्रिएको छ, पन्ध्र नापले फरक परेको गल्ती हतारमा पाटीको पछाडि सच्याएर कोरिएको भेटिन्छ ।

पाँच हजार वर्ष पुरिएको त्यो गल्तीले कुनै पनि स्मारकले गर्न नसक्ने काम गरिदिन्छ । त्यसले कुसिमलाई हामीजस्तै मान्छे बनाइदिन्छ । चिनेजानेको बनाइदिन्छ । कुनै किंवदन्ती होइन, कामको चटारोमा हिसाब अलिकति बिगारेको साधारण एक मान्छे ।

कुसिम इतिहास लेखिरहेको थिएन । ऊ जौ गनिरहेको थियो, आफ्नो काम गरिरहेको थियो ।

कुसिम इतिहास लेखिरहेको थिएन । ऊ जौ गनिरहेको थियो, आफ्नो काम गरिरहेको थियो ।

इतिहासमा पहिलोपटक लेखिएकी महिला

कुसिमको पाटीभन्दा एक-दुई पुस्तापछिको अर्को पाटी छ, करिब स.पू. ३१०० को । यसमा एक जना मालिक र उसले दुई दास किनेको टिपोट भेटिन्छ ।

                गल-सलका दुई दास- एन-पप (काटिएको) र सुक्कलगिर (En Pap X, Sukkalgir) 

चार शब्दमा तीन जना- एउटा मालिक, र उसले दास बनाएका दुई मान्छे । एन-पपको नामको एउटा भाग काटिएको छ, हामीले अझै पढ्न सकेका छैनौँ । उसको आधा नाम बाँचेको छ । उसैसँग जोडिएको अर्को नाम छ- सुक्कलगिर, जसबारे कुनै सन्देह छैन ।

अहिलेसम्मको पुरातात्त्विक अभिलेखले नाम पढ्न मिल्ने पहिली महिला उनै हुन् । कुनै देवी होइनन् । कुनै रानी होइनन् । मन्दिरको भित्तामा कुँदिएकी पुजारी पनि होइनन् ।

सम्पत्ति ।

गल-सलका दुई दासहरू- सिकागो म्युजियम OIM A2513, (फोटो, जिन ग्रान्ट) ।

अभिलेखले हामीलाई दिएको कुरा यही हो, र यसलाई अडिएर हेर्नु वेश हुन्छ । संसारमा पहिलोपटक कुनै महिलाको नाम लेखिँदा, उनी कसको सम्पत्ति हुन् भनेर हिसाब राख्नलाई लेखिएको हो ।

संसारमा पहिलोपटक कुनै महिलाको नाम लेखिँदा, उनी कसको सम्पत्ति हुन् भनेर हिसाब राख्नलाई लेखिएको हो ।

उनले त्यो लेखिनन् । उनको भनाइ केही थिएन । उनी कस्ती थिइन्, कसरी अरुको भइन्, कति बाँचिन्- हामीलाई थाहा छैन । हामीलाई उनको नाम थाहा छ, र गल-सलले उनलाई दास बनाएको थियो भन्ने थाहा छ ।

अनि, निशाको कुरा

इतिहासमा भेटिने पहिलो मान्छेको कथा सुनाउने धेरै ठाउँमा तपाईंले पहिलो महिलाको नाम भनेर निशा भेट्नुहुनेछ- कुसिमकी हाकिम, उनका खातामा सही गर्ने महिला, इतिहासमा नाम लेखिएकी पहिली महिला ।

राम्रो कथा हो । तर, यसमुनि कुनै अध्ययनको आधार छैन । जहाँ भेटिन्छन्, त्यहाँ प्रायः नि ‘स्सा’ लेखिएको हो कि भनेर अनुमान हुन्छ, निशा होइन । उनी महिला थिइन् भन्ने कुनै प्रमाण भेटिँदैन । कथा एकपटक सुनाउँदा र अर्कोपटक सुनाउँदाको बीचमा कतै उनी बनिएकी हुन् जस्तो देखिन्छ ।

साँचो कुरा गाह्रो हुन्छ । प्रायः यस्तै हुन्छ ।

चित्रबाट अक्षर

सुमेरमा सभ्यताको सुरुवात भर्खरै हुँदै थियो । स.पू. ३००० आइपुग्दा उरुक प्राचीन् समयको सबैभन्दा ठूलो शहर भइसकेको थियो- करिब ५० हजार- १ लाख स्थायी बासिन्दा बस्ने शहर ।

कुसिमको केही पुस्ताभित्रै ती चित्रहरू फेरिन थालिसकेका थिए । बिस्तारै पिक्टोग्राफहरू सरल हुँदै गए । आवश्यकताले माटोका पाटीमा खोपिएका चित्रलाई बिस्तारै अक्षर बनाइदियो ।

मेसोपोटामियाको गर्मीमा दिनको सयौँ कागज सार्ने लेखकसँग माछा भन्नुपर्दा हरेकपटक माछा कोर्ने फुर्सद हुँदैन । चित्र सजिलो बन्दै जान्छ । चिनो घुम्छ । साँढेको टाउको फेरिएर धर्को मात्रै बन्छ, जसलाई कसैले साँढे भनेर चिन्दैन ।

स.पू. ३००० सम्ममा लिपि चित्रबाट पूरै हटेर माटोमा कोणमा ठोकिएका चुच्चा छापहरूमा पुगिसकेको थियो, जसलाई हामी अहिले क्युनिफर्म भन्छौँ । अनि, चिनोको सङ्ख्या पन्ध्र सयभन्दा माथिबाट झरेर करिब छ सयमा आइपुगेको थियो ।

अक्षरले आवाज बोक्न थालेपछि

त्यसबेला कसैले बुझ्यो- माटोको पाटीमा कोरिएका अक्षरले आवाज जनायो भने । माछाको चित्रले माछा होइन, माछाभन्दा निस्कने आवाज । टाउकोको चित्रले टाउको होइन, त्योभन्दा निस्कने अक्षरांश ।

अनि, अक्षरले आवाज जनाउन सक्छ भने त्यसलाई आवाज भएको जुनसुकै शब्दका लागि प्रयोग गर्न सकिने भयो । अनि, जुनसुकै शब्दका लागि अक्षर हुन सक्छ भने, लेखिएका पाटीहरू जुनसुकै विचार बोक्न सक्ने भए ।

तर, यो नयाँपनसँगै अर्को कुरा पनि भित्रियो- पहुँचको साँघुरोपन । यी नयाँ चिनो पढ्न र लेख्न पढेलेखेका लेखकहरूको एउटा वर्गले मात्रै सक्थ्यो । एउटा पेसा जन्मियो । लेखिएको शब्दको वरिपरि चुपचाप ठूलो-सानोको एउटा तह बस्यो, अनि संसार फेरि पहिलेजस्तो भएन ।

किनभने, पहिलोपटक ज्ञानले बोली र सम्झनाभन्दा लामो आयु पायो । माटो सुक्यो, अक्षर बाँचिरह्यो । त्यसैले हामी अहिले पनि तिनका महाकाव्य पढ्न सक्छौँ, तिनको सङ्गीतको प्रतिध्वनि सुन्न सक्छौँ । मान्छेले आफू जन्मिनुभन्दा सयौँ वर्षअघि मरिसकेका राजा र लेखकबाट सिक्न पाए । अधिकार बोलेर मात्रै होइन, सारेर पनि दिन सकिने भयो । ज्ञान सम्झेर मात्रै राख्नुपर्ने भएन, त्यसमाथि थप्न सकिने भयो ।

सुमेरको प्रविधि भर्खरै सुरु हुँदै थियो । मेसोपोटामिया वरिपरि फैलिएको मानव-सभ्यताको प्रारम्भिक विन्दु यही थियो ।

अन्त्यमा, फेरि उही पर्खाल

कुसिमले जौको हिसाब बिगारेको केही शताब्दीपछि, त्यही शहरका लेखकहरूले माटोमा एउटा राजाको कथा कोर्दै थिए । त्यो राजा, जो संसारको छेउसम्म पुगेर रित्तै फर्किएको थियो । जो आफ्नै पर्खालअगाडि उभियो, अनि आफ्नै अस्थायित्व बुझ्यो ।

कुसिमको जौ उहिल्यै खाइसकियो । उरुकका पर्खाल अहिले भग्नावशेष मात्र छन् । गिल्गामेस मरेको पाँच हजार वर्ष भयो । तर, तिनका नाम अझै छन् । गिल्गामेसको महाकाव्य गिल्गामेस मरेको छ सय वर्षपछि लेखिएको थियो, अनि एक हजार वर्षपछि त्यही कथाले तोराह बाइबल र कुरान जन्मायो ।

अनि, भेटाएका सुरुवाती नामहरूमध्ये एउटी महिलाको पनि नाम छ- सुक्कलगिर ।

संसारमा पहिलोपटक कुनै महिलाको नाम लेखिँदा उनलाई कसैको सम्पत्ति भनेर लेखिएको थियो । उनले लेखिनन् । उनको भनाइ त्यहाँ केही थिएन । किनबेचको हिसाबकिताबको दाबी- सम्पत्ति मात्रै ।

पाँच हजार वर्षपछि पनि आज हामी कुसिम, एन-पप र सुक्कलगिर पढ्न सक्छौँ । जौ गन्ने एउटा मान्छे । एउटा पुरुष, जसको आधा नाम मात्रै बाँचेको छ । अनि एउटी महिला, जसको नाम कसैले आफ्नो सम्पत्तिको हिसाब गर्दा लेखिएको थियो ।

लेखाइले गरेको यही हो- सम्झनालाई जोगाइदियो । यसले शक्तिशालीलाई मात्रै जोगाएन, यसले होसियारलाई पनि जोगायो । यसले शक्तिविहीनहरूलाई पनि जोगायो ।

धेरैले सोध्ने प्रश्न

इतिहासमा लेखिएको सबैभन्दा पुरानो नाम कुन हो?

हामीले पढ्न सक्ने सबैभन्दा पुरानो नाम सायद कुसिम हो। उरुकका स.पू. ३४०० देखि ३१०० बीचका अठारवटा हिसाबका पाटीमा यो नाम छ। तर यो कुनै मान्छेको नाम हो कि पदको, विद्वान्‌हरू अझै पक्का छैनन्।

नाम पढ्न मिल्ने पहिली महिला को हुन्?

सुक्कलगिर। स.पू. ३१०० तिरको एउटा पाटीमा गल-सल नाम गरेका मालिकका दुई दासमध्ये एकको रूपमा उनको नाम लेखिएको छ।

एक घण्टामा ६० मिनेट किन हुन्छ?

सुमेरका मान्छे साठीको आधारमा गन्थे। एउटा हातका चार औँलाका १२ गाँठा बुढीऔँलाले गनेर, अर्को हातका पाँच औँलाले दर्जन गन्दा साठी पुग्छ। त्यही प्रणाली बेबिलोन हुँदै आजको घडी र वृत्तसम्म आइपुग्यो।

किलाकार (क्युनिफर्म) लिपि कहिले सुरु भयो?

उरुकमा स.पू. ३४०० तिर चित्रलिपि (प्रोटो-क्युनिफर्म) सुरु भयो। स.पू. ३००० सम्म ती चित्र माटोमा कोणमा थिचिएका चुच्चा चिनोमा बदलिए, जसलाई हामी किलाकार भन्छौँ।

के निशा इतिहासमा नाम लेखिएकी पहिली महिला हुन्?

होइन। ‘निशा’ को कथा इन्टरनेटमा धेरै फैलिएको छ, तर यसको कुनै अध्ययनको आधार छैन, र उनी महिला थिइन् भन्ने प्रमाण पनि छैन।

यो पनि पढ्नुहोस्

  • संसार डुबाएको पुरानो बाढीको कथा
  • समयको उत्खनन शृङ्खलाका अरू लेख
  • यो लेख अङ्ग्रेजीमा पढ्नुहोस् (English)
  • भोकभन्दा पहिले आस्था! जब मन्दिरले गाउँ र खेती जन्मायो

title.$t: Roman Britannia, Part IV: The Long Goodbye

content.$t:
How Rome left Britain, and what it left behind- The End of Roman Britannia and the work of the giants.

In 410 CE, an emperor hiding in Ravenna sent a letter to Britain's cities with a simple message: look to your own defense. But Rome's exit isn't a sudden collapse; it is a tale of ambitious usurpers slowly bleeding the island of its legions to fight for the throne.

From the elevation of an ordinary soldier to the arrival of Anglo-Saxons who wandered through the ruins, Part IV explores the melancholic end of an empire and the "work of giants" it left behind.

Coin of Constantine III, 407–411 CE. An ordinary soldier elevated by the British legions because of his name.

In short

  • From Carausius in 287 CE to Magnus Maximus in 383 CE, Britain’s armies kept crossing the Channel to make emperors.
  • After 306 CE, Constantine the Great took British legions east. They were never fully replaced, but Christianity stayed.
  • In 407 CE, the legions chose a soldier named Constantine. Constantine III took the last garrison to Gaul and was executed in 411.
  • Around 410 CE, Emperor Honorius told Britain’s cities to defend themselves. Roman Britain ended with a letter, not a battle.
  • Anglo-Saxon settlers found the ruins and, in the Old English poem The Ruin, called them enta geweorc, “the work of giants”.

407 CE: A Military Camp in Northern Britannia

It had happened before. That was the point.

The legions of Britain had done this twice already in the past year alone. They had raised a soldier named Marcus on a shield and called him emperor. When Marcus disappointed them, they killed him and raised a man named Gratian.

When Gratian disappointed them within four months, they killed him too. Now they needed a third candidate.

The Western Empire was collapsing around them. Barbarians had crossed the frozen Rhine on the last day of 406 CE in the largest single migration the empire had ever seen. Gaul was burning. The legitimate emperor, Honorius, had retreated behind the impregnable marshes of Ravenna and showed no sign of coming out.

The British legions looked at the chaos across the Channel and made a decision. They wanted a name. Not a strategy. Not a general of proven brilliance. A name.

A century earlier, in this very province, a man named Constantine had been raised on a shield by British legions, and that Constantine had gone on to conquer the entire Roman world. The soldiers of Britain had developed something close to a superstition about it.

The name felt like a formula. Raise a Constantine, win the world.

They looked around the camp. They found a soldier. An ordinary soldier, nobody famous, nobody distinguished, no military record that survives in any source. But his name was Constantine.

They raised him on a shield.

He immediately stripped the last garrison from the island, crossed the Channel, and was dead within four years.

Britain never got its soldiers back, and Roman Britannia died with Constantine the Third.

The formula had worked once. That was the problem. Once is enough to make a tradition, and traditions in the Roman army had a way of outlasting their reasons.

I. The Pattern: A Century of Warlords

Coin of Carausius, self-proclaimed Emperor of the Britannic Empire, 287–293 CE. A naval commander who held Britain and northern Gaul against Rome for nearly a decade.

The century between Albinus and Constantine III had confirmed, again and again, that Britain was less a province than a launching pad.

After the catastrophe of 197 CE, after Albinus’s army had been butchered at Lugdunum and the northern Wall stripped bare, it took the personal intervention of the emperor Septimius Severus to stabilize the province. He arrived in 208 CE, old and gouty, and launched brutal punitive campaigns deep into Scotland.

Septimius died in York in 211 CE, the same city where Constantine would later be proclaimed. His sons Caracalla and Geta promptly abandoned their father’s Scottish ambitions and made peace with the northern tribes.

However, the damage had been done. The northern tribes had seen the Wall empty. They burned the forts and proved the frontier was permeable. Rome had lost the psychological advantage it had spent decades building.

In 260 CE, a breakaway Gallic Empire briefly incorporated Britain into its territories, three separate emperors governing a rump western empire for fifteen years, while the legitimate court struggled in the east.

In 287 CE came the most audacious episode of all: a naval commander named Carausius, facing prosecution for corruption, declared himself emperor of Britain and northern Gaul. He issued his own coins. He maintained his own court. He controlled the Channel fleet and defied Rome for seven years until his own minister had him murdered.

His successor lasted another three years before the emperor Constantius, father of Constantine the Great, mounted a military expedition and brought Britain back under central control.

Each episode followed the same grammar. A strong commander. A large army. A fractured empire. A crossing of the Channel. And Britain, once again, was left to manage itself in the interim, stripped of soldiers, exposed to the north, working out its own arrangements.

The island was becoming adept at self-sufficiency. That would matter in the end.

II. The Emperor from the Island: Constantine and the Christian World

Chi-Rho mosaic, Hinton St Mary, Dorset, c.350 CE, British Museum. The earliest known image of Christ from Roman Britain.

Constantine the Great, proclaimed in York in 306 CE, changed the world. But what did he do for Britain?

The British Problem demanded it. Constantine could not stay in Britain and be content. The very pattern that had made him emperor made staying impossible. The Tetrarchy, the system of four co-emperors Diocletian designed to prevent exactly this kind of provincial coup, had given legitimate succession to Galerius, the senior Augustus in the east.

Statue of Constantine: a bronze statue of Constantine the Great in York, the very city where he was proclaimed emperor in 306 CE before marching south to claim the Roman world.

Galerius had not appointed Constantine. The British legions had. That made Constantine a usurper under Roman law, regardless of his father’s bloodline. His only path to legitimacy was conquest.

He had to take the whole empire or lose his head. The same isolation that made Britain a breeding ground for emperor-makers also made it a trap: a man proclaimed in York could be dismissed as a provincial warlord unless he moved fast, moved south, and proved himself in the arena that actually counted.

The British Problem, in other words, did not just create Constantine. It chased him out of Britain. The province that handed him his purple had to strip its legions to fund the campaign that would make him real. Britain lost its emperor the same way it always did, by having him cross the Channel and never come back.

In the short term, he left. Britain was the platform, not the destination. He took his British legions east, fought his way across Gaul and Italy, and in 312 CE at the Milvian Bridge outside Rome, defeated his last serious rival under the sign of the Chi-Rho, the Christian symbol he claimed had appeared to him in a vision the night before battle. He legalized Christianity, convened the Council of Nicaea, founded Constantinople, and became the most consequential emperor since Augustus.

Britain received Christianity in return. The faith had been spreading quietly through the province for decades. Roman Britain shifted from a province with a patchwork of mystery cults, local gods, and a growing Christian minority to a province with an established church.

Christianity would prove to be the most durable thing Rome left in Britain. Constantine’s conversion made it official.

Christian communities existed in the larger towns, and British bishops attended the Council of Arles in 314 CE. Long after the administrators left, the coins stopped coming, and the villas were stripped for building stone, the church remained.

But the legions Constantine took east in 306 CE were never fully replaced. The garrison thinned. The Wall was still manned, the towns still functioning, the villas still occupied, but the depth of military resources that made Britain feel like a functioning part of the empire was quietly, steadily ebbing.

III. Magnus Maximus: The Second March

Coin portrait of Magnus Maximus, proclaimed emperor by the British legions in 383 CE. Remembered in Wales as Macsen Wledig, the last Roman who felt like theirs.

The clearest preview of the end came in 383 CE.

Gratian was the son of Valentinian I, a competent soldier-emperor who had kept the western frontiers intact through sheer professional force of will. When Valentinian died in 375 CE, power in the west passed to Gratian, who was sixteen. He grew into a ruler not without ability, but he inherited an empire in crisis and possessed none of his father’s iron authority.

The catastrophe arrived in 378 CE. The Goths, granted refuge inside the Danube frontier by a corrupt Roman administration, rose in revolt. At the Battle of Adrianople, the eastern emperor Valens, Gratian’s uncle, rode into a Gothic ambush and was killed. The Roman army of the east was effectively destroyed. It was the Roman Empire's worst military defeat at the time.

What followed hardened the western legions' contempt for Gratian. He responded to the Gothic crisis not by crushing the Goths but by negotiating with them, granting them unprecedented terms in 382 CE that allowed them to settle as a semi-autonomous people and owe Rome only loose military service.

To soldiers who had spent their careers dying to hold the line, this looked like surrender. Worse still, in the eyes of the traditional army, was what Gratian surrounded himself with. He showed marked personal favor to a unit of Alanic cavalry, steppe nomads; dressing in their style, hunting with them, lavishing them with gifts. To the Roman soldiery, this was not merely eccentric. It was a humiliation. Their emperor preferred barbarians to them.

In Britain, Magnus Maximus watched all of this from the far end of the empire. He was a capable, experienced Spaniard, deeply popular with the troops who had served under him for years along the Wall. When the chance came, his soldiers made the familiar calculation and proclaimed him Augustus.

End of Roman Britannia, 383–410 CE.

Maximus crossed to Gaul, defeated and killed Gratian, and established himself as western emperor. He ruled competently for five years, governing from Trier, negotiating with the Franks and Visigoths, and holding the Rhine frontier against relentless pressure.

By most measures, Maximus was a better emperor than the man he replaced. But Maximus stripped Britain’s garrison to fight his continental war, and that came with a heavy price.

And in 388 CE, the eastern emperor Theodosius marched west, defeated him in battle, and had him executed. The troops Maximus had taken from Britain never returned.

The Western Empire he left behind was unstable and diminished. Gratian’s younger brother Valentinian II was restored as western emperor in name, but Theodosius held the real power. When Valentinian II was found dead in 392 CE, almost certainly murdered by his powerful Frankish general Arbogast, the general installed a pagan professor named Eugenius as a puppet emperor and governed through him.

Theodosius marched west again. At the Battle of the Frigidus in 394 CE, he defeated Arbogast and Eugenius in one of the century's most bitterly fought engagements. Eugenius was executed. Arbogast fell on his sword. Theodosius became, briefly, the last man to rule the entire Roman Empire alone.

He died in 395 CE, leaving the empire to his two young sons. Arcadius, seventeen, received the east. Honorius, ten years old, received the west. The division was supposed to be administrative, not permanent. It proved to be both. The empire was never reunified.

And the soldiers that Maximus had taken from Britain were gone, absorbed into continental wars, deployed along the Rhine and the Danube, buried on Italian hillsides. Britain would make do with what was left.

There was always somewhere the soldiers were needed more. The eastern frontier. The Danube. The Rhine. Gaul. Spain. Italy. Britain waited at the end of the list, and the list never got shorter.

IV. The Last Constantine: 407 CE

The Western Roman Empire, c.410 CE. Britain sits at the fraying edge of a world dissolving from within. Honorius told its cities to defend themselves. No reinforcements were promised. No governor was named. That was the last official communication.

Which brings us back to the ordinary soldier with the fortunate name.

By 407 CE, the Britain that remained was diminished. The great villa estates of the south were fewer and quieter than they had been a century before. Coin circulation had been steadily declining since the 360s.

The towns still stood. The Wall was still, nominally, garrisoned. The administrative structures of the Diocese of Britannia still functioned. But the connection to Rome was fraying at every edge, and everyone in the province who paid attention knew it.

Constantine III crossed to Gaul in 407 CE with what remained of Britain’s garrison. He had early success; he stabilized the Rhine frontier, smashed the previous winter, gathered support in Gaul and Spain, and for a moment looked like he might be the real thing. He controlled more territory than most of his predecessors.

Coins of Constantine III.

But 407 CE was also the year the Visigoths under Alaric were circling Italy. And in 410 CE came the event that stunned the Roman world: Alaric sacked Rome itself. The eternal city, symbol of everything the empire meant, fell to a barbarian army for the first time in eight hundred years. The psychological shock was total.

Jerome wrote from Bethlehem that he could not speak for tears. Augustine began writing The City of God, an entire theology designed to explain why Rome's fall did not mean the fall of meaning.

By 411 CE, Honorius's forces had captured and executed Constantine III. The soldiers he had taken from Britain were dead, dispersed, or absorbed into other units.

The Diocese of Britannia, four provinces, administered from London, garrisoned along Hadrian’s Wall, integrated into the tax system and economy of the western empire for nearly four centuries, quietly ceased to function as a Roman entity.

In that same catastrophic year of 410 CE, the emperor Honorius sent a letter to the cities of Britain. The letter told the British cities to defend themselves.

No reinforcements were promised. No new governor was appointed. No timeline was given for restoring Roman authority. In the precise, bureaucratic language of imperial administration, the letter told the cities of Britain they were on their own.

That was all. This is how Roman Britannia ended. Not with a battle. Not with an invasion.

With a letter. With silence. With the slow absence of the coins that no longer arrived on the supply ships that no longer came.

V. The Silence and What Followed

Portchester Castle, Hampshire, a Saxon Shore fort built by the Romans c.285 CE to defend against Germanic raiders.

The fall of Roman Britain was not an event. It was a slow, uneven process, stretching across generations and visible only in retrospect.

The towns did not immediately empty. The villas did not immediately collapse. The roads kept working because roads keep working; they require no maintenance to remain usable for decades.

The Christian church survived better than the imperial administration that had legitimized it. The language shifted gradually, British Latin giving way to the older Celtic tongues, then, over the following centuries, to the Germanic dialects of newcomers from across the North Sea.

The newcomers had been coming for years. Germanic warriors- Angles, Saxons, Jutes, Frisians- had been raiding the eastern coast of Britain for generations.

The Romans had called this coastline the Saxon Shore and built a chain of massive forts specifically to defend against them. Now no one manned the forts. The walls still stood. The gates still swung. But the garrison was gone, and the coast was open.

Some came as raiders. Some came as settlers, invited by sub-Roman British rulers who needed warriors and had land to offer. Some came simply because the land was available and no organized military force was defending it. The process took generations, not years. In the west, Wales, Cornwall, Cumbria, parts of the north, Romano-British culture persisted for a century or more after the administrative end of Roman rule.

But across the lowland east, the heartland of Roman Britain, the land of villas and forums and heated floors and colonnaded basilicas, the transformation was eventually total.

The towns were gradually abandoned or occupied in ways that left no trace in the Roman building stock. The villas fell into disrepair, their roofs collapsing inward, their mosaic floors buried under the slow accumulation of rubble, soil, and time. The forum of Londinium, once the largest north of the Alps, became a field.

And then the Anglo-Saxons walked among the ruins.

VI. The Work of Giants

The Great Bath, Aquae Sulis (Bath), Somerset. The sacred hot springs channeled, roofed, and monumentalized by Rome. The steam never stopped rising. The people who built the roof were gone before anyone thought to write their names down.

They didn't know who built them.

The Anglo-Saxon settlers who moved through the abandoned landscapes of what had been Roman Britain looked at the stone walls, the crumbling basilicas, the bathhouses with their mysterious underfloor cavities, and the great roads running straight and true to the horizon, with no framework for understanding any of it.

Nothing in their world was built from dressed stone. Nothing in their experience suggested that human hands could have raised structures on this scale.

They called them enta geweorc. The work of giants.

An anonymous Anglo-Saxon poet, writing sometime in the 8th or 9th century, three hundred years after the last Roman administrator had left, stood before the ruins of Roman Bath, Aquae Sulis, and tried to put into words what they saw.

The poem has come down to us damaged and incomplete, half-eaten by time, missing whole passages. We call it The Ruin. What survives is one of the most quietly devastating things ever written in English.

Wrætlic is þes wealstan, wyrde gebræcon,
burgstede burston, brosnað enta geweorc.
Wondrous is this masonry, broken by fate,
the city-places have crumbled, the work of giants decays.

The poet described roofless halls and fallen towers. The frost on the stones. The place where men had once laughed and drunk and glittered with gold. They described the hot springs still steaming, still running, still warm, three centuries after the last Roman had used them, as though the earth itself remembered what had been built above it and refused to forget.

The poet had no word for Roman. No concept of the empire that had built this, governed this, garrisoned this, taxed this, Christianized this, and then, exhaustedly, bureaucratically, with a letter nobody quite remembers sending, let go of this.

They saw only the evidence of a greatness they could not name, in a language that carried no memory of what had made it. And they wrote it down.

That act, the Anglo-Saxon poet standing in the ruins and recording their wonder at the work of giants, is the strange, melancholy full stop at the end of Roman Britain. Four centuries of roads and walls and law and language and religion, of olive oil from Spain and wine from Gaul and letters home complaining about the cold, reduced in human memory to the evidence of a vanished race of builders.

Rome came to Britain not to liberate it, not to love it, not to stay. It came to extract, to garrison, to tax, and in the end, to leave. What it built in the leaving was something it never intended: a people practiced in surviving without it.

What remained, the roads still running, the walls still standing, the hot springs still steaming, the church still singing in Latin to congregations who no longer spoke it, the genes and place-names and legal habits and crop rotations quietly absorbed into the fabric of an island, was the ghost of an occupation that had lasted longer than the United States has yet existed.

The Anglo-Saxon poet stood in the ruins and marveled at the work of giants.

We are still, in some sense, standing in it.
